items.title: South Central 98: Key developments in protests and crackdown in Delhi
items.summary: Were Saurav Das and Ashutosh detained for breaching a peace bond, or were preventive powers being used to restrict their right to protest? In this week’s South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Pooja Prasanna examine the legal questions surrounding the detention of Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the use of peace bonds and the limits of the state’s power to prevent protests. They are joined by Apar Gupta, advocate and founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, to discuss the role of executive magistrates, preventive detention and the implications for the right to dissent. The discussion examines how executive magistrates can require people to sign peace bonds to maintain public order, and what happens when authorities subsequently detain them for allegedly violating those conditions. It also looks at the distinction between preventing a possible breach of peace and using preventive powers to restrict people’s freedom to protest. Apar Gupta questions the legality of the detentions, arguing that the authorities’ actions in this case were unlawful and that the two men should have been released. items.title: Peace bonds: The colonial tool rearing its head amid protests in 2026
items.summary: In 2023, the Indian parliament enacted three new penal laws: the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), in place of its colonial era ancestors, a move that Union Home Minister Amit Shah said would make the criminal justice system "completely Swadeshi" . Back then, lawyers criticised the "new" statues as "old wine in a new bottle", largely retaining many problematic provisions introduced in colonial times. In 2026, the means adopted by the British Raj of quelling dissent still remain firmly cemented in Indian penal procedures. The recent nationwide protests and the police response to them put these provisions under the spotlight, especially those that deal with preventive policing. Detained protestors were made to sign bonds promising not to cause "breach of peace" for varying amounts of time. Here, we give historical context to these peace bonds, show how they have been retained in current jurisprudence and speak to leading criminal law practitioners on the issue. items.title: Constitutional lawfare and why courts must stay away from political interest litigation
items.summary: Lawfare is a term that has increasingly been used since the turn of this century to describe the use or misuse of courts and legal institutions to achieve a desired political or military objective. The term has been employed to denote the use of law and legal systems against indigenous populations of the United States of America. It has also been used in the international military context to characterise/demonise legal actions brought against military actions of the USA and Israel. While a more traditional understanding of lawfare denotes powerful actors delegitimising the less powerful who are seeking rights and accountability, in India, lawfare could assume another dimension. A slew of recent such judicial actions would make this clearer. On October 5, the Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register a criminal case to probe corruption allegations involving Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann's office. What is noteworthy is that the order was passed on a public interest litigation (PIL) filed by advocate Nikhil Saraf. State of UP ]. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran censured the State police for fabricating a case without basic investigative steps. "The State Police would do well to educate their officers in the process of investigation...Six years have been erased from the life of a man on the strength of a concocted story built on mere surmises and conjectures. Not even a rudimentary investigation was carried out...The investigation and prosecuting agencies exist not merely to, and by whatever means bring in a conviction," the Bench remarked. It observed that the botched investigation put an innocent citizen’s life and liberty into serious jeopardy. "This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person’s life and liberty...We were appalled at the manner in which the investigation was carried out," the Bench noted. items.title: Life Insurance Guide for South Indians: How to Buy the Right Plan in 2026
items.summary: Buying life insurance in 2026 takes about as long as ordering groceries, which is both the good news and the trap. The purchase is easy; the decision still deserves care. This is a working guide for the urban South Indian professional who wants to get it right in one sitting: what to buy, in what order, and the five steps from decision to policy document. Step One: Decide the Job to Be Done Every life insurance product answers one of two needs. Income replacement if you die, which is protection. Or a disciplined pot of money if you live, which is saving. Protection is urgent and comparatively inexpensive; saving is important and has many competitors. So the sequence is fixed: a large pure term insurance cover on the earning member first, sized at 10 to 15 times annual income plus outstanding loans 1 , and only then any savings-oriented policy for named goals like education, a home or retirement. Step Two: Know the 2026 Advantages Two recent changes tilt the maths in the buyer’s favour. GST is not applicable on individual life insurance premiums, so a quoted premium is the amount you actually pay. items.title: Print, Scan and Copy: Does a College Student Need an All-in-One Printer?
items.summary: Your assignment is ready, but the print shop has closed. Tomorrow, you also need a copy of your college ID and a scanned signature for an internship application. These small jobs can make owning a printer tempting. But convenience alone does not settle the decision. Some students print every week; others submit almost everything online. An all-in-one printer for college students makes sense when printing, scanning and copying are regular needs. If they are rare, campus facilities and a phone scanner may be enough. What Does an All-in-One Printer Actually Do? An all-in-one printer combines three functions in one machine: ● It prints digital files, such as assignments, reading material and application forms. ● It scans paper documents into digital files for saving or uploading. ● It copies an existing paper document without requiring you to recreate it on a computer. You can therefore print a report, save a signed form as a PDF and photocopy a receipt using the same device. However, each function has limits.
